content: Access to HIV prevention, treatment, and care for individuals who inject drugs remains a critical public health priority. Updated guidelines from 2012 emphasize the importance of universal access to these services, particularly in vulnerable populations such as those in prisons or other closed settings. Comprehensive intervention packages have been developed to address the unique needs of these populations, including harm reduction strategies and access to antiretroviral therapy (ART). For sex workers in lowand middle-income countries, targeted HIV and sexually transmitted infection (STI) prevention and treatment programs are essential. Practical approaches to implementing these programs have been outlined, focusing on collaborative interventions to improve health outcomes in this group. People living with HIV who are co-infected with viral hepatitis often experience more severe liver disease, including higher rates of cirrhosis, hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), and mortality. Early diagnosis of viral hepatitis co-infection in HIV-positive individuals is crucial, as is the provision of ART and specific antiviral therapies. Direct-acting antiviral (DAA) therapies for hepatitis C virus (HCV) have shown comparable outcomes in HIV co-infected individuals as in those with HCV mono-infection, with cure rates exceeding 95%, even in cases of prior treatment failure or advanced fibrosis. This has eliminated the need to consider HIV/HCV co-infected patients as a particularly difficult-to-treat population. Hepatitis B virus (HBV) vaccination is especially important for HIV-infected adults, as they are at higher risk of HBV infection. All newly diagnosed HIV patients should be screened for HBV markers (HBsAg and anti-HBs) to identify chronic HBV infection and determine vaccination needs. However, the response to HBV vaccination may be lower in HIV-positive individuals, particularly those with low CD4 counts. A four-dose schedule of double-strength (40 µg) HBV vaccine has been shown to provide better protection than the standard three-dose schedule. In settings with high prevalence of tuberculosis (TB), intensified TB case-finding should be integrated into HIV, HBV, and HCV testing services. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends a four-symptom screening algorithm (cough, weight loss, fever, and night sweats) to rule out active TB. If symptoms are present, further investigations are necessary. Drug interactions are a significant concern in individuals co-infected with HIV, HBV, or HCV who are receiving antituberculosis treatment. Drug-induced liver injury is three to six times more common in these populations. While all DAA regimens interact with rifampicin, no serious interactions are anticipated between sofosbuvir or daclatasvir and multidrug-resistant (MDR) or extensively drug-resistant (XDR) TB regimens. Migrant and mobile populations, including refugees, asylum seekers, and migrant workers, are particularly vulnerable to HBV, HCV, and HIV infections. These groups often face barriers to accessing healthcare due to stigma, language differences, discrimination, and legal challenges. Efforts to improve testing uptake in these populations should address these barriers and provide culturally appropriate education on hepatitis and HIV risks. Routine testing for HBV and HCV, along with HBV vaccination for non-immune healthcare workers, should be standard practice. Testing and prevention strategies for couples, partners, and household contacts of individuals with chronic HBV infection can efficiently identify additional cases and reduce transmission risks. Partner testing for HIV and viral hepatitis is increasingly offered in various settings, including antenatal care and community-based services. Pregnant women should be universally tested for HBV, and in high-endemic settings, HCV testing should also be considered. The most effective strategy to prevent mother-to-child transmission (MTCT) of HBV is administering the first dose of the HBV vaccine within 24 hours of birth, followed by timely subsequent doses. Antiviral therapy during the third trimester may further reduce MTCT risk in HBV-infected pregnant women. For HCV, while MTCT rates are lower than for HBV, the risk increases significantly in HIV co-infected mothers. Children born to HBVor HCV-positive mothers should be routinely tested and monitored for signs of liver disease. In endemic regions, HBV is predominantly transmitted perinatally or in early childhood, while HCV transmission is often linked to maternal infection. Testing for HBV in exposed infants should occur at 12 months of age, while HCV infection in children under 18 months can only be confirmed through virological assays due to the presence of maternal antibodies. Special considerations are needed for vulnerable adolescents, such as those living on the streets or engaged in high-risk behaviors. Strategic planning for hepatitis testing services should involve a situational assessment of national and subnational epidemiology, testing coverage, and barriers to access. Programs should prioritize populations and geographic areas with high prevalence and unmet needs, ensuring linkage to care and treatment. Monitoring and evaluation of testing activities are critical to optimize program effectiveness and public health impact.
